objective: Scarcity arises because unlimited wants exceed limited resources (time, money, land, labor, capital).；Four factors of production: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.；Production Possibility Curve (PPC) shows maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with fixed resources and technology.

learningGoals.statement: Understand scarcity and opportunity cost concepts and apply them to economic choices.

knowledgeNodes.name: Scarcity
knowledgeNodes.definition: The fundamental economic problem of having seemingly unlimited human wants in a world of limited resources.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.

knowledgeNodes.name: Factors of Production
knowledgeNodes.definition: The resources used to produce goods and services: land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (machinery, tools, buildings), and entrepreneurship (risk-taking, innovation).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Analyse aspects of economic growth/development, including its costs, benefits, and sustainability.

knowledgeNodes.name: Production Possibility Curve (PPC)
knowledgeNodes.definition: A model showing the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with fixed resources and technology; illustrates scarcity, opportunity cost, and efficiency.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.

knowledgeNodes.name: Opportunity Cost
knowledgeNodes.definition: The value of the next best alternative that must be foregone when making a choice; measured on a PPC as the amount of one good given up to produce more of another.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.

knowledgeNodes.name: Efficiency on PPC
knowledgeNodes.definition: Points on the PPC are allocatively efficient (full resource use); points inside are inefficient (underutilized resources); points outside are unattainable with current resources/technology.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.

miniLesson.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when making a choice. It is not always money; it can be time, leisure, or any benefit you forgo. Every choice involves a trade-off because resources are scarce.
miniLesson.example: Xiao Qiang gave up a $40,000 salary to open a shoe store. The opportunity cost of opening the store is the $40,000 salary he could have earned, not the rent or other expenses. The rent is an explicit cost, but the opportunity cost is the forgone alternative.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of opportunity cost as the road not taken—what you gave up, not what you paid.

guidedPractice.prompt: If you choose to attend college instead of working a full-time job that pays $30,000 per year, what is the opportunity cost of attending college?
guidedPractice.answer: $30,000 per year in forgone salary (the next best alternative).

guidedPractice.prompt: You have $100 and three options: buy a concert ticket for $80, buy a textbook for $100, or have dinner with friends for $50. If you choose the textbook, what is the opportunity cost? (Assume the concert ticket is your next best alternative.)
guidedPractice.answer: The opportunity cost is the concert ticket valued at $80, because that is the next best alternative you give up.

guidedPractice.prompt: On a PPC for corn and wheat, moving from point A (100 corn, 0 wheat) to point B (80 corn, 20 wheat). What is the opportunity cost of producing 20 more units of wheat?
guidedPractice.answer: The opportunity cost is 20 units of corn (the amount of corn given up to produce the additional wheat).

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects option other than C on question 'diag-cia4u-s6-q3' or does not demonstrate understanding in question 'diag-cia4u-s6-q5'
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may confuse points inside, on, and outside the PPC, e.g., thinking a point inside is unattainable or a point outside is efficient.

miniLesson.explain: The Production Possibility Curve (PPC) shows maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with fixed resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient (full resource use). Points inside the curve are inefficient (resources underutilized). Points outside the curve are unattainable with current resources and technology.
miniLesson.example: On a PPC for corn and wheat: point A on the curve means you produce efficiently; point B inside means you produce less than possible (e.g., some workers idle); point C outside is impossible right now (e.g., you'd need more land or better seeds).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Inside = Inefficient (idle resources); On = Optimal (efficient); Outside = Out of reach (unattainable).

guidedPractice.prompt: On a PPC for computers and phones, a point inside the curve is: efficient, inefficient, or unattainable?
If a country produces 10 wheat and 5 corn (point inside the PPC), what must happen to reach the curve? Explain using opportunity cost.
guidedPractice.answer: The country must use idle resources (e.g., hire unemployed workers). Moving to the curve has zero opportunity cost because you can produce more of both goods without giving up anything.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student says: 'A point outside the PPC is efficient because it shows high output.' Correct the error and explain why it's impossible.
guidedPractice.answer: The student is wrong. Points outside the PPC are unattainable with current resources and technology; they are not efficient. Efficiency only applies to points on the curve. To reach an outside point, the economy would need more resources or better technology.

reteachModules.trigger: student selects any option other than B on question 'diag-cia4u-s6-q4'
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may not distinguish between a parallel shift (overall resource increase) and a rotation (productivity improvement in one good).

miniLesson.explain: A Production Possibility Curve (PPC) can change in two ways: a shift or a rotation. A parallel shift outward occurs when the economy gains more resources (e.g., more land, labor, capital) or overall technology improves for both goods. A rotation occurs when productivity improves for only one good, expanding that good's maximum output while the other good's maximum stays the same. For example, if wheat productivity doubles due to new technology, the PPC rotates outward along the wheat axis; corn maximum remains unchanged. This illustrates that the PPC is not static and changes differently based on the source of growth.
miniLesson.example: Using the wheat and corn example, if a new farming technique doubles wheat output per acre but doesn't affect corn, the PPC rotates outward on the wheat axis. The new point shows more wheat can be produced at any given corn level, but the maximum corn is unchanged.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a table: if you make the whole table bigger, it's a shift. If you only extend one side of the table, it's a rotation. PPC shift = entire curve moves outward; PPC rotation = one axis expands.

guidedPractice.prompt: A country's PPC for cloth and wheat shifts outward equally for both goods. What likely caused this change?
guidedPractice.answer: An overall increase in resources (e.g., more labor) or technology improvement affecting both industries.

guidedPractice.prompt: If a new irrigation system boosts only corn production, does the PPC shift or rotate? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: It rotates outward along the corn axis because only corn's maximum output increases, while wheat's maximum stays the same.

guidedPractice.prompt: An economy produces computers and cars. A new robot improves car assembly but not computer production. Describe the change to the PPC and explain the opportunity cost of producing more cars.
guidedPractice.answer: The PPC rotates outward along the cars axis. The opportunity cost of producing one more car is the number of computers given up, which may change at different points on the curve.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected an option other than B on diagnostic question: 'Scarcity in economics refers to:'
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often think scarcity means shortage, poverty, or temporary high prices, rather than the fundamental economic condition of unlimited wants vs limited resources.

miniLesson.explain: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: our wants (for goods, services, time, etc.) are unlimited, but the resources (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) to fulfill them are limited. This forces us to make choices. Scarcity is not the same as poverty—even wealthy people face scarcity because they cannot have everything they want, and time is scarce for everyone. It also applies to non-physical things like time and services.
miniLesson.example: Consider Xiao Qiang, who must decide between opening a shoe store or keeping his job. He has limited time and money. Even if he were rich, he would still face scarcity of time—he cannot work two full-time jobs. Similarly, a student has only 24 hours a day to study, sleep, and socialize. That is scarcity.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Scarcity = unlimited wants + limited resources. Like trying to fill a bucket with a tiny faucet—you can never satisfy all wants.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following best defines scarcity in economics?
guidedPractice.answer: Unlimited human wants exceeding limited resources.

guidedPractice.prompt: Give a real-world example of scarcity that does not involve poverty or money.
guidedPractice.answer: A student has only 24 hours in a day but wants to study, exercise, and socialize—time is scarce.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why scarcity is considered the fundamental economic problem and how it leads to opportunity cost.
guidedPractice.answer: Because wants are unlimited but resources are limited, people must make choices; every choice has an opportunity cost—the next best alternative given up.

questions.stem: You have two hours after school. You can either work a part-time job earning $15 per hour, or volunteer at an animal shelter (no pay, but you value the experience). If you choose to work, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The $30 you earn from working
The experience of volunteering at the shelter
The time you spend working
The cost of transportation to work

questions.stem: Explain why opportunity cost is not always measured in money. Provide an example from your own life or from the lesson to support your explanation.
questions.rubric: Student must: (1) correctly define opportunity cost as the value of the next best alternative foregone (1 point); (2) provide a clear example where the next best alternative is not monetary (e.g., time, leisure, satisfaction) (1 point); (3) explain why the cost is not money in that example (1 point). Total 3 points.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer the multiple-choice question correctly and score at least 2 out of 3 points on the open-ended question.

questions.stem: A farmer uses all available land and labour to produce apples and oranges. A point on the PPC represents 100 apples and 50 oranges. A point inside the curve represents 60 apples and 30 oranges. Which statement is correct?
options: The inside point is unattainable because the farmer could produce more.
The inside point is efficient because all resources are used.
The inside point is inefficient because some resources are idle.
The inside point is outside the curve and therefore impossible.

questions.stem: A country produces only two goods: healthcare and education. Its current PPC shows a point outside the curve representing 100 healthcare units and 200 education units. A politician claims this point is both efficient and achievable. Explain why the politician is wrong, and state what would need to change for that point to become attainable.
questions.rubric: The student must explain that a point outside the PPC is unattainable with current resources and technology (not efficient). To make it attainable, the country would need more resources (e.g., higher labour force, more capital) or technological improvements that shift the PPC outward. Full credit for correctly identifying that points outside are unattainable and not efficient, and for naming at least one way to shift the PPC outward.

retestCards.passRule: Must answer the multiple-choice question correctly, and the open-ended response must correctly classify the point as unattainable and explain the need for resource/technology increases.

questions.stem: A nation produces corn and wheat. A new fertilizer increases wheat yield per acre by 20% but has no effect on corn. Which statement best describes the change to the nation's Production Possibility Curve (PPC)?
options: The PPC shifts outward equally for both goods.
The PPC rotates outward on the wheat axis, increasing the maximum wheat while corn maximum stays the same.
The PPC rotates outward on the corn axis, increasing the maximum corn while wheat maximum stays the same.
The PPC does not change because fertilizer is not a resource.

questions.stem: An economy produces only computers and cars. A new technology improves only car assembly, doubling the number of cars that can be produced per hour, but does not affect computer production. Describe how the economy's PPC changes (shift or rotation, and along which axis). Then explain what happens to the opportunity cost of producing one more car compared to before the technology change.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies that the PPC rotates outward along the cars axis (axis label can be cars or car axis). Explanation: Opportunity cost of a car is the number of computers foregone; because only car production capacity increased, the slope of the PPC changes: at given levels of car output, fewer computers are given up to produce an additional car (or opposite, depending on point). For full credit, student must specify rotation on car axis and note that opportunity cost decreases (or changes) because the trade-off improves.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer (index 1) for the multiple-choice question AND provide an open-ended response that correctly identifies rotation on the cars axis and explains a change in opportunity cost (e.g., lower opportunity cost per car due to productivity gain).

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates the economic concept of scarcity?
options: A family cannot afford a new car due to low income.
A billionaire cannot buy more than 24 hours in a day.
A store runs out of a popular product during a sale.
A country experiences a shortage of oil due to war.

questions.stem: Explain why a student who has to choose between studying for a test and going to a party is facing scarcity. What is the opportunity cost of choosing to study?
questions.rubric: Student must identify that the student has limited time (scarcity) and unlimited wants (study and party). Opportunity cost of studying is the enjoyment and experience of the party (the next best alternative foregone).

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly.

Unattainable points lie outside the curve. Inside is attainable but inefficient.
✓ Correct. Points inside the PPC indicate the economy is not using all its resources fully.
Maximum output is achieved on the curve, not inside.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that a point inside the PPC means inefficient resource use.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.alignmentNote: PPC efficiency is a direct application of OE B1's concept of scarcity and choice.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think a point inside the PPC is efficient or unattainable.

cards.question: If a country discovers a new technology that doubles wheat production but does not affect corn production, the PPC will:
options: Shift outward for both goods equally
Rotate outward along the wheat axis
Rotate outward along the corn axis
Not change
cards.diagnosis: Test whether students distinguish between a general resource increase and a productivity gain in one sector.
misconceptions: A parallel shift requires an overall increase in resources or productivity in both sectors. Here, only wheat productivity improves.
✓ Correct. The maximum wheat output increases while corn max stays the same, so the curve rotates on the corn axis.
Rotation along the corn axis would mean corn productivity increased, not wheat.
Technology change expands production possibilities, so the PPC must shift outward in some way.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that a technology improvement affecting only one good rotates the PPC.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.alignmentNote: PPC shifts are part of understanding resource allocation under scarcity (OE B1).
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think any improvement shifts the whole PPC outward equally.

cards.question: Using the concepts of efficiency and opportunity cost, explain why a point inside the PPC is undesirable and how a society could move to a point on the curve.
cards.diagnosis: Assess ability to synthesize PPC concepts: efficiency, opportunity cost, and resource allocation.
cards.successCriteria: Student explains that a point inside the PPC is inefficient due to underutilized resources and moving to the curve requires using idle resources, referencing opportunity cost.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.alignmentNote: Evaluating PPC points involves deeper understanding of scarcity and efficiency (OE B1).
cards.commonMisconception: Students may not connect inefficiency with opportunity cost or may not identify what 'moving to the curve' entails.
